subtype: Approach: asks several friends for suggestions [Action]
passage: Tejas wanted a name for the village cricket team, and "Team Tejas" did not sound right. After school he sat under the banyan tree with a stub of pencil and a torn page. He asked five friends one by one, and then his cousin Pankaj, who had come for the harvest week. "Thunder Bulls." "Super Sixers." "Dhoop Dhamaka." "Lazy Langurs." And Pankaj said, "Mango Tigers." Tejas wrote all six names in a column and read them out to the group, watching faces. Mango Tigers made everyone laugh, even the boy who had suggested the Bulls. "That's ours," said Tejas, and drew a tiger holding a bat.

qa.q: Who did Tejas ask besides five friends?
qa.a: Tejas also asked his cousin Pankaj.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel about the name "Team Tejas" at the start?
qa.a: Tejas felt it did not sound right, so he was not satisfied and wanted a name that everyone would like.

qa.q: What could Tejas do if two names got equal laughs?
qa.a: Tejas could ask the players to vote by raising hands, so the team decides together.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel when Mango Tigers was chosen?
qa.a: Pankaj may feel proud and happy, since Pankaj's idea was picked.

grounding: Shows a boy asking five friends and a cousin for team names, writing them all down and choosing the one that made everyone laugh.

subtype: Approach: polls a class group for options [Action]
passage:
'Thirty replies,' Damini said, holding up her phone in the canteen. 'I asked the class group what to give Mrs Rao for the farewell.'

'Thirty? Show me,' said Kavitha.

'Look. Photo album, plants, a mug, a card everyone signs, a scarf, a video of wishes...'

'That's a lot of different things.'

'That's why I made piles. Five of them: memories, plants, useful things, something to wear, and something homemade. Memories has eleven votes if you count the album, the video and the signed card.'

'So we pick from memories?'

'First we ask everyone which pile they like, then we choose inside it.'

Kavitha grinned. 'Can I do the video?'

'You're on it.'

qa.q: How many replies did Damini collect?
qa.a: Damini collected thirty replies.

qa.q: How does Kavitha seem to feel about the video?
qa.a: Kavitha seems keen and happy, grinning and asking to do the video.

qa.q: What could Damini do if the class disagrees about which pile to choose?
qa.a: Damini could ask everyone to vote for a pile in the group, and combine two ideas if it is close.

qa.q: How might a classmate who suggested the scarf feel?
qa.a: That classmate may feel a little disappointed if it is not chosen, but included, since every idea was counted and sorted.

grounding: Shows a student asking the class group for gift ideas, collecting thirty replies and sorting them into a few themes.

subtype: Approach: collects suggestions from a wide community and looks for repeated patterns [Thinking]
passage:
'Sixty-two replies,' Jagdish said, scrolling. 'On the fresher post. Everyone wrote something different.'

Avni pulled the laptop closer. 'Bus timings. Library cards. Mess timings. The wifi password.'

'Wait,' said Jagdish. 'Read the ones I highlighted.'

'"Didn't know the gate closes at ten." "Nobody told me visitors aren't allowed." "Confused about laundry days."'

'All hostel rules,' said Jagdish. 'Fourteen of the sixty-two, more than any other topic. When the same thing turns up again and again from different people, it's not luck.'

'So orientation needs a hostel rules session?'

'Or one page. But first we check with the warden that these rules are the current ones.'

qa.q: How many of the replies mentioned hostel rules?
qa.a: Fourteen of the sixty-two replies mentioned hostel rules.

qa.q: What does Jagdish seem to feel about the repeated hostel replies?
qa.a: Jagdish feels sure and interested, having spotted a pattern that many freshers share.

qa.q: What could the club do with the hostel finding?
qa.a: The club could check the current rules with the warden, then add a short hostel session or a one-page sheet to orientation.

qa.q: How might a fresher who was confused about laundry days see the new session?
qa.a: That fresher would probably feel relieved that someone listened and cleared up the rules early.

grounding: Shows a club collecting online replies about orientation and noticing that many mention confusion about hostel rules.

subtype: Approach: takes the most upvoted idea without checking it fits [Pitfall]
passage:
Subject: The flavour launch

Dear Shankar,

You asked how the new flavour is doing, so here is the honest answer. Last month I posted a poll asking which jam flavour to launch next. It got nine hundred votes, and chocolate mango won by miles. I ordered the ingredients, ran two big batches and printed labels. Only then did I check who had voted. Most were strangers who follow the page for funny videos, and hardly any had ever bought from me. My regular customers, mostly families ordering for the week, like mild lime and ginger. In three weeks I have sold eleven jars of chocolate mango. The rest sit on my shelf. I trusted the number and never asked who was behind it.

Maria

qa.q: How many jars of the new flavour has Maria sold in three weeks?
qa.a: Maria has sold eleven jars of chocolate mango in three weeks.

qa.q: How does Maria feel about having trusted the poll?
qa.a: Maria feels regretful and a little foolish for trusting the number without asking who was behind it.

qa.q: What could Maria do before launching a flavour next time?
qa.a: Maria could ask regular customers directly, or offer small tasting jars to buyers, before making big batches.

qa.q: How might a regular customer see the new flavour?
qa.a: A regular customer might find it odd or unnecessary, since regular buyers like mild flavours for family meals.

grounding: Shows an owner adopting the most-voted poll choice although the voters were not customers, and the product not selling.

subtype: Approach: weighs the answers by who gave them and tests the top few [Revision]
passage: Latika's home bakery in the colony had collected three hundred suggestions for a new cake. She opened her order register and marked the names of people who had bought from her at least twice: forty-one. Their ideas were eggless orange and date-and-walnut. Vijay, who helped with deliveries, said, "Try both, small." She baked ten of each on Saturday, labelled them new, and set them by the counter. By evening the orange cake was gone and four of the date-and-walnut were left. "The buyers picked," said Vijay. Latika added eggless orange to the weekly menu and kept a note of the other result in her book.

qa.q: How many people had bought from Latika at least twice?
qa.a: Forty-one people had bought from Latika at least twice.

qa.q: How did Latika likely feel about running a small test rather than one big batch?
qa.a: Latika likely felt cautious and curious, wanting to see which cake buyers would actually pick, not only suggest.

qa.q: What could Latika do if both cakes sell out next time?
qa.a: Latika could put both on the menu in alternate weeks and note which one gets reordered more.

qa.q: How might Vijay see the small batch test?
qa.a: Vijay might find it sensible and low-risk, since the test was cheap and the buyers gave a clear answer.

grounding: Shows an owner keeping only suggestions from real customers, testing two in small batches and keeping the one buyers pick.

subtype: Approach: works out what each side wants and finds a swap [Thinking]
passage:
In the flat in Singapore, Chen and Yuki both stood at the study table with their homework. "It's mine, I need it at four," said Chen. "No, I need it at four too," said Yuki. Then Yuki stopped. "Wait. Why do you want four?"

"The window makes it bright in the afternoon, and my drawing needs light."

"Oh. I don't need light. I need quiet, and four o'clock is noisy because of the school bus."

Chen thought about it. "After dinner it's quiet. You could have it then."

"And you take the afternoon until dinner?"

They wrote it on a sticky note: Chen 4 to 6, Yuki 7 to 9. Mama stuck it on the table with a smile.

qa.q: What times did they write on the sticky note?
qa.a: They wrote Chen 4 to 6 and Yuki 7 to 9.

qa.q: How did Yuki feel after learning why Chen wanted the afternoon?
qa.a: Yuki felt relieved and understanding, since the two needs turned out to be different.

qa.q: What could they do if Chen needs more than two hours for drawing?
qa.a: They could talk again and find another bright spot for part of the drawing, or trade a weekend afternoon, using what each of them needs.

qa.q: How might Mama see the sticky note?
qa.a: Mama may feel pleased and relieved that the two settled it themselves.

grounding: Shows two siblings asking what each really needs from the study table and agreeing on split hours.

subtype: Approach: separates a demand from the interest behind it [Thinking]
passage: Nilesh's fists were tight as he rehearsed in the lift. Papa, I'm staying at Rohit's till ten. No. Last time he had said "It's my life", and Papa's face had closed like a door. So why did Papa say no? It was not about the friend, since Papa liked Rohit. It was the late bus and the dark stretch near the flyover. "The worry is the ride home," he told himself. "Not the party." That was a problem he could solve. At dinner he said, "Papa, can I stay till ten? Sumit bhaiya lives near Rohit's, and he said he'll bring me back on his scooter. He has a spare helmet." Papa looked at Mummy. "Ask Sumit to text me when you leave." "Done," said Nilesh.

qa.q: Who offered to bring Nilesh back?
qa.a: Sumit bhaiya said he would bring Nilesh back on his scooter.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when he first rehearsed the request in the lift?
qa.a: Nilesh felt tense and defensive, with tight fists, expecting to hear a no.

qa.q: What else could Nilesh offer his parents?
qa.a: Nilesh could text when he arrives and when he leaves, so his parents know he is safe.

qa.q: How might Papa see Nilesh's changed request?
qa.a: Papa may feel relieved that the travel worry is settled, and glad that Nilesh listened to it.

grounding: Shows a teenager working out that his parents' worry is the ride home and offering a safe lift.

subtype: Approach: prepares options and a fallback before talking [Action]
passage:
'Before anyone gets annoyed,' Parul said, putting three sheets on the table, 'I made options.'

'Options for what?' asked Kishore.

'The chores. Option one: a weekly rota, one job each. Option two: swap jobs every month. Option three: pay a helper for the bathroom and split the cost.'

'That last one feels expensive.'

'Then we drop it. I can live with the first two, but not with everyone doing what they feel like.'

Kishore laughed. 'So the fallback is a rota?'

'Yes. If we can't agree on the swap, we start the rota on Monday.'

'Rota's fine,' called their third flatmate from the sofa.

'Fine,' said Kishore. 'Rota with a monthly swap?'

'Deal.'

qa.q: How many options had Parul written down?
qa.a: Parul made three options.

qa.q: How does Parul seem to feel going into the talk, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Parul seems calm and prepared, since Parul offered options, knew what was acceptable and did not argue when one was rejected.

qa.q: What could Parul do if the roommates reject all three options?
qa.a: Parul could ask what each roommate finds hard about chores and shape a fourth option together.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel about the meeting?
qa.a: Kishore may feel relaxed and respected, since the choices were laid out and the objection to the costly one was accepted.

grounding: Shows a student preparing several rota options and a fallback so the chores talk with roommates stays calm.

subtype: Approach: treats it as winner takes all and damages the relationship [Pitfall]
passage:
Thursday night. Asked Farida to swap Saturday's shift so I could go to my cousin's engagement. Farida said, "Sorry, can't." Asked two others. Same answer. Nobody even looked up. It stings. Three weeks ago I insisted the release schedule stay my way, with testing on Mondays. I brought numbers and made sure everyone knew I was right. I won. Nobody argued after that. Since then people hand me tasks on the shared board without a word and have stopped coming to my desk. Farida told me back then, "It only works for you." I said the numbers say otherwise. Tonight I think I won the argument and lost something else. Maybe I should ask what Monday testing costs them.

Sandeep

qa.q: What did Farida say when asked to swap the shift?
qa.a: Farida said, "Sorry, can't."

qa.q: How does Sandeep feel now?
qa.a: Sandeep feels hurt and uneasy, saying that it stings and that something else was lost.

qa.q: What could Sandeep do to repair things with colleagues?
qa.a: Sandeep could ask colleagues what Monday testing costs them and look for a schedule that works for everyone.

qa.q: How might Farida have seen the original schedule fight?
qa.a: Farida may have felt unheard, having said it only worked for Sandeep, and later unwilling to do favours.

grounding: Shows a team member winning a schedule argument by insisting, then finding colleagues stop cooperating and refuse favours.

subtype: Approach: asks what the other side needs and reshapes the deal [Revision]
passage:
With four days left before the festival fair, Madhuri and Arnab had argued for an hour over the price of a hundred tote bags. Madhuri said she could not go above her budget. Arnab said he could not go lower. The clock in the workshop seemed to tick louder.

"Stop," said Madhuri. "Let me ask something else. What matters most to you in this deal?"

Arnab rubbed his forehead. "Honestly? Cash by Friday. My cloth supplier wants payment then, and I'm short."

"If I pay half now and half on delivery, can you come down on the price?"

He counted on his fingers. "Yes. Ten rupees less per bag."

They shook hands. The bags were packed on Thursday, and both were relieved.

qa.q: What did Arnab need by Friday?
qa.a: Arnab needed cash by Friday.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel during the stalemate?
qa.a: Madhuri felt frustrated and pressed for time, as the argument went nowhere while the days ran down.

qa.q: What could Madhuri do if Arnab still cannot lower the price?
qa.a: Madhuri could offer something else Arnab values, such as a repeat order or quicker pick-up, in return.

qa.q: How might Arnab see the trade?
qa.a: Arnab may feel relieved, since early payment solved the supplier problem.

grounding: Shows a buyer asking what matters most to a vendor after a stalemate and trading earlier payment for a lower price.
